ID: 401 Text: Teagasc is confirming that the coming days will see the completion of most disease control programmes in winter wheat and spring barley crops. ID: 402 Text: Meanwhile, the start of the 2026 harvest continues to draw ever closer. Recent rains have served to boost crop growth rates. ID: 403 Text: What is required now are a few dry weeks to get the combines rolling. ID: 404 Text: According to Teagasc agronomists, septoria levels have been very low up to this point, as a result of all the dry weather in late May. ID: 405 Text: Yellow rust has been an issue in some crops, mainly those that did not receive a leaf four application and can still be seen in crops on the flag leaf. ID: 406 Text: Meanwhile, the final ‘head’ spray helps to top up control of disease on the flag leaf. ID: 407 Text: It gives some protection against fusarium and other ear diseases, especially if the weather is broken during flowering. ID: 408 Text: Growers should time the final fungicide application at early flowering, which is normally three weeks after the flag leaf spray. ID: 409 Text: Many of the March drilled crops have already received their final fungicide. ID: 410 Text: However, most of the later sown crops still have to receive their final application. ID: 411 Text: Late season disease control in spring barley is designed to control ramularia and diseases such as rynchosporium or net blotch. ID: 412 Text: Agronomists are confirming that ramularia will probably be an issue this year due to the weather conditions in May, ranging from cold north winds in the first half of the month to record temperatures at the end of the period. ID: 413 Text: While different varieties have differing levels of tolerance to ramularia, being able to predict which varieties are going to show signs of infection is very difficult. ID: 414 Text: For this reason, we would recommend that growers protect all barley crops from ramularia. ID: 415 Text: Repeated trials have clearly shown that from flag leaf fully emerged to the awns peeping is the optimum timing for applying the final fungicide to spring barley crops. ID: 416 Text: However, waiting for the heads to come fully out and to start flowering (i.e. 10 -14 days later) can reduce yields by 0.3-0.4t/ha. ID: 417 Text: This yield loss clearly shows that allowing ramularia to develop in the crop makes it more difficult to control, so earlier applications of fungicides are important. ID: 418 Text: This is because all the products that are available will only work preventatively; they will not cure it when it is visible. ID: 419 Text: Therefore, by applying a fungicide early, growers are trying to delay the infection from occurring for as long as possible, thus keeping the crop greener for longer. ID: 420 Text: Shearing is one of the busiest days of the year on sheep farms. ID: 421 Text: However, by completing a couple of simple tasks beforehand, the job can be made that little bit easier. ID: 422 Text: Teagasc has shared key tips from David Heraty of the Irish Wool Council aimed at not only making the job easier on the sheep, the farmer and the shearer, but to also ensure the presentation of wool is improved. ID: 423 Text: Heraty said this is an "important factor in improving the value of the product produced". ID: 424 Text: He stressed that it is "important to shear the sheep well to obtain the highest quality wool". ID: 425 Text: His key takeaways are: ensure sheep are dry and fasted; separate lambs from ewes to reduce stress and fleece soiling; remove dags to keep the wool clean; and arrange for extra help to manage sheep and wool handling. ID: 426 Text: Heraty advises to house and fast sheep the night before shearing. ID: 427 Text: "This ensures sheep are empty the next morning, reducing stress for both the animals and the shearer," he explained. ID: 428 Text: "Ideally, sheep should be housed on slatted floors or accumulated winter bedding rather than fresh straw, which can stick to the fleece. ID: 429 Text: "If housing is not possible, keep sheep in a bare paddock." ID: 430 Text: Step two involves drafting ewes from lambs. ID: 431 Text: Heraty said drafting ewes from lambs facilitates easier movement of ewes. ID: 432 Text: "Ewes will be anxious to return to the lambs and this will reduce the risk of fleeces becoming soiled," he said. ID: 433 Text: Next, remove dags from ewes prior to shearing. ID: 434 Text: "Dagging beforehand reduces extra work and prevents contamination of the wool during shearing," he said. ID: 435 Text: Heraty added that having extra help available on shearing day "makes the task that little bit easier". ID: 436 Text: "One person can focus on handling the sheep, while the other manages the wool," he said. ID: 746 Text: Disease control in spring bean crops must be addressed by growers over the coming days, according to Teagasc. ID: 747 Text: Foliar diseases such as chocolate spot, downy mildew and rusts need to be controlled in order for crops to keep the foliage for as long as possible. ID: 748 Text: All diseases develop quickly in warm, humid conditions. ID: 749 Text: For chocolate spot control, fungicides need to be applied before the disease develops. Therefore, growers should apply a fungicide at the first signs of disease or in any case at the start of flowering and repeat two to three weeks later. ID: 750 Text: Signum 0.5-0.75kg/ha can be applied at both timings for good control. Elatus Era is also an option and has approval for a single application on beans at 0.66L/ha. ID: 751 Text: For downy mildew control, there are no fungicides currently available that will give control, however, Basfoliar Active and Nutriphite PGA - which are bio-stimulants - both claim to give some control. ID: 752 Text: Meanwhile, beans offer growers a good opportunity to control problematic grass weeds such as bromes, ryegrasses, and wild oats with graminicide-type herbicides. ID: 753 Text: Good control can be achieved where products such as Fusilade Max (1.0 – 3.0L/ha), Stratos Ultra (1.5 – 4.0L/ha), or Falcon (0.7 -1.5L/ha) are used in time. ID: 757 Text: Preventing seed return of grass weeds like blackgrass, Italian ryegrass, or wild oats has to be the first line of defence for next year’s crop. ID: 758 Text: Where populations are low, rogueing should be carried out. However, where populations are too high for manual control then spot spraying with glyphosate has to be considered.
